categories.name: Yourself: culture and investment
categories.blurb: As the leader, you set cyber strategy, fund it, and build a culture where security is a shared priority.

categories.name: Your staff: awareness and vigilance
categories.blurb: Your people are the first line of defense, so train them to spot threats and make safe choices online.

categories.name: Your systems: protect assets and apps
categories.blurb: Know what hardware and software you run, keep it updated and supported, and retire what puts you at risk.

categories.name: Your surroundings: the digital workplace
categories.blurb: Make sure only the right people and devices can reach your systems, with strong sign-in and least privilege.

categories.name: Your data: backups and recovery
categories.blurb: Know what information matters, back it up regularly, and protect those backups so you can recover after loss.

categories.name: Your crisis response: limit damage
categories.blurb: Plan ahead so that when an incident hits you can contain the damage and restore normal operations quickly.

questions.text: Do you treat cybersecurity as a business risk and factor it into your strategic and financial planning?
questions.why: When leaders ignore cyber risk, the organization underinvests and stays exposed to avoidable attacks.
questions.fix: Add cybersecurity as a standing item in your business planning and risk discussions.

questions.text: Have you budgeted for and invested in basic cybersecurity tools, services, and staff?
questions.why: Without dedicated funding, essential protections go unimplemented and gaps persist.
questions.fix: Set aside a defined portion of your budget for cybersecurity and review it each cycle.

questions.text: Do you know which of your critical business operations depend on IT systems and data?
questions.why: If you cannot map operations to the systems behind them, you cannot protect what matters most.
questions.fix: List your core business functions and note the IT systems and data each one relies on.

questions.text: Have you led the creation of written cybersecurity policies for your organization?
questions.why: Without clear policies, staff make inconsistent decisions and security expectations go unmet.
questions.fix: Draft and approve baseline policies covering acceptable use, access, and incident reporting.

questions.text: Do you take part in information-sharing networks with industry peers and government agencies?
questions.why: Isolated organizations learn about threats too late to act on early warnings.
questions.fix: Join a sector information-sharing group or subscribe to CISA alerts and advisories.

questions.text: Are cybersecurity roles and responsibilities clearly assigned to specific people in your organization?
questions.why: When no one owns security tasks, they fall through the cracks and accountability is lost.
questions.fix: Name who is responsible for each key security duty and communicate it across the team.

questions.text: Do you regularly review your cyber risks and adjust priorities as threats change?
questions.why: A one-time assessment goes stale as your business and the threat landscape evolve.
questions.fix: Schedule a recurring review of your top cyber risks and update your priorities accordingly.

questions.text: Do you provide regular cybersecurity awareness training to all employees?
questions.why: Untrained staff are more likely to fall for attacks that bypass technical defenses.
questions.fix: Roll out a recurring awareness training program for everyone, including new hires.

questions.text: Does your training teach staff how to recognize phishing emails and social engineering?
questions.why: Phishing is a leading entry point for attackers, and unaware staff click without hesitation.
questions.fix: Include phishing examples and red flags in training, and consider simulated phishing tests.

questions.text: Do employees know how and to whom they should report a suspected cyber incident?
questions.why: Delayed reporting lets small incidents grow into major breaches before anyone responds.
questions.fix: Publish a simple reporting path and remind staff that early reporting is encouraged.

questions.text: Have you built a workplace culture that encourages and rewards secure online behavior?
questions.why: If security feels like a burden, staff cut corners and risky habits spread.
questions.fix: Recognize good security behavior and make safe choices the easy, expected default.

questions.text: Do you keep staff informed about current cyber threats affecting your industry?
questions.why: Staff cannot stay vigilant against threats they have never heard about.
questions.fix: Share timely alerts about active scams and attacks hitting your peers or sector.

questions.text: Does your training cover ransomware and the risks of malicious links and attachments?
questions.why: One careless click on a malicious file can trigger ransomware that halts your operations.
questions.fix: Teach staff to verify senders and avoid opening unexpected links or attachments.

questions.text: Do you tailor cybersecurity training to the specific risks each role faces?
questions.why: Generic training misses the targeted threats aimed at finance, IT, or executive staff.
questions.fix: Add role-specific guidance for higher-risk positions on top of general training.

questions.text: Do you maintain a current inventory of the hardware connected to your network?
questions.why: You cannot secure or patch devices you do not know are on your network.
questions.fix: Build and regularly update a list of all devices connected to your network.

questions.text: Do you maintain a current inventory of the software and applications your organization uses?
questions.why: Unknown or unmanaged software can hide vulnerabilities that attackers exploit.
questions.fix: Track every application in use and remove anything unneeded or unauthorized.

questions.text: Are automatic updates enabled for operating systems and third-party software where possible?
questions.why: Unpatched software leaves known holes open for attackers long after fixes exist.
questions.fix: Turn on automatic updates across operating systems and applications where available.

questions.text: Do you apply security patches promptly after they are released?
questions.why: Attackers move quickly to exploit newly disclosed flaws before they are patched.
questions.fix: Set a target timeframe for testing and deploying critical patches after release.

questions.text: Have you replaced or retired operating systems, applications, and hardware that are no longer supported?
questions.why: End-of-life technology stops receiving security fixes and becomes an easy target.
questions.fix: Identify unsupported systems and plan to upgrade or replace them.

questions.text: Do you install software only from trusted, legitimate sources?
questions.why: Software from unverified sources can carry malware straight into your systems.
questions.fix: Restrict installs to vetted vendors and official app stores or repositories.

questions.text: Do you consider security when selecting vendors and third-party technology in your supply chain?
questions.why: A weak vendor or component can become the path attackers use to reach you.
questions.fix: Ask vendors about their security practices before adopting their products or services.

questions.text: Do you keep an inventory of the users and devices that have access to your network?
questions.why: Unknown users or devices with access can move through your systems undetected.
questions.fix: Maintain a current list of who and what is authorized on your network.

questions.text: Have you enabled multi-factor authentication for all users?
questions.why: A stolen password alone lets an attacker in unless a second factor blocks them.
questions.fix: Turn on multi-factor authentication for email, remote access, and key accounts.

questions.text: Do you grant access and administrative rights based on least privilege and need-to-know?
questions.why: Excess privileges let a single compromised account cause widespread damage.
questions.fix: Give each user only the access their role requires and remove the rest.

questions.text: Do you require unique passwords for each account rather than shared logins?
questions.why: Shared or reused credentials make it impossible to trace actions and easy to breach many accounts at once.
questions.fix: Eliminate shared accounts and encourage a password manager for unique credentials.

questions.text: Do you promptly disable accounts and revoke access when someone leaves or changes roles?
questions.why: Lingering accounts for former staff are a common way attackers slip back in.
questions.fix: Tie account deactivation to your offboarding and role-change processes.

questions.text: Do you have written procedures for adding, changing, and removing user access?
questions.why: Without a defined process, access changes are missed and permissions drift out of control.
questions.fix: Document how access is requested, approved, changed, and revoked.

questions.text: Do you separate everyday user accounts from privileged administrator accounts?
questions.why: Using admin accounts for daily work means routine mistakes can hand attackers full control.
questions.fix: Give administrators separate standard accounts for everyday tasks.

questions.text: Do you know what sensitive or critical information is stored across your systems?
questions.why: You cannot protect or back up data you have not identified and located.
questions.fix: Inventory where your critical and sensitive information lives.

questions.text: Do you run regular, automated backups of your critical data and systems?
questions.why: Without recent backups, ransomware or hardware failure can cause permanent data loss.
questions.fix: Set up scheduled, automated backups of your important data and systems.

questions.text: Do you keep at least one backup copy offline or otherwise isolated from your network?
questions.why: Backups connected to your network can be encrypted or deleted in the same attack.
questions.fix: Store at least one backup copy offline or in isolated, immutable storage.

questions.text: Are your backups encrypted and physically protected from unauthorized access?
questions.why: Unprotected backups can be stolen or read, exposing all the data they contain.
questions.fix: Encrypt backup media and store it in a physically secured location.

questions.text: Do you regularly test that your backups can be restored successfully?
questions.why: A backup that fails to restore is worthless in the moment you need it most.
questions.fix: Periodically perform a test restore to confirm your backups work.

questions.text: Do you use malware protection to defend the data on your devices and network?
questions.why: Malware can corrupt, steal, or lock up your data before you notice anything is wrong.
questions.fix: Deploy and keep current antivirus or anti-malware tools on your devices.

questions.text: Do you securely erase data from devices before disposing of or reusing them?
questions.why: Discarded drives that still hold data can leak sensitive information to whoever finds them.
questions.fix: Wipe or destroy storage media before devices leave your control.

questions.text: Have you developed a written incident response plan for cyber attacks?
references: CISA Cyber Essentials: Your crisis response
questions.why: Without a plan, people improvise under pressure and small incidents spiral out of control.
questions.fix: Write a basic incident response plan covering roles, steps, and contacts.

questions.text: Do you have a disaster recovery plan to restore operations after a disruption?
references: CISA Cyber Essentials: Your crisis response
questions.why: Without a recovery plan, downtime drags on and losses mount after an incident.
questions.fix: Document the steps and resources needed to bring critical systems back online.

questions.text: Do you know who to contact for help during a cyber incident, including law enforcement and vendors?
references: CISA Cyber Essentials: Your crisis response
questions.why: Scrambling to find help mid-crisis wastes time when every minute matters.
questions.fix: Prepare a contact list of internal leads, vendors, insurers, and authorities.

questions.text: Do employees know the internal steps for reporting and escalating an incident?
references: CISA Cyber Essentials: Your crisis response
questions.why: If staff do not know how to escalate, warnings never reach the people who can respond.
questions.fix: Share a clear internal escalation path and make sure everyone understands it.

questions.text: Have you identified which systems and operations to prioritize when restoring service?
references: CISA Cyber Essentials: Your crisis response
questions.why: Without set priorities, recovery efforts scatter and the most vital functions stay down longer.
questions.fix: Rank your critical systems so you know what to restore first.

questions.text: Do you practice or exercise your response and recovery plans regularly?
references: CISA Cyber Essentials: Your crisis response
questions.why: Plans that are never rehearsed tend to fail when a real incident strikes.
questions.fix: Run a tabletop exercise to walk through your plans and find the gaps.

questions.text: Do you review and update your response plans after incidents or major changes?
references: CISA Cyber Essentials: Your crisis response
questions.why: Outdated plans reflect systems and contacts that no longer exist when you need them.
questions.fix: Update your plans after each incident, exercise, or significant business change.
